messages.author: 051b8654c3457b56
messages.subject: ddply(.. transform ..) but for aggregation
parts:
Hi,

I only recently discovered, inside the ggplot2 book, the great syntax with transform() to get ddply to add a new column with per-group computed values, akin to SQL windowing functions.  E.g.:

> x=movies[movies$year %in% c(2000,2005), c('title','year','rating')] d=rbind(x[x$year==2000,][1:2,], x[x$year==2005,][1:2,])
> d
                title year rating
6               $pent 2000    4.3
72            ...Lost 2000    6.2
79  ...al fin, el mar 2005    5.0
402    37 og et halvt 2005    5.6

> ddply(d, .(year), transform, mean_rating_by_year = mean(rating))
              title year rating mean_rating_by_year
1             $pent 2000    4.3                5.25
2           ...Lost 2000    6.2                5.25
3 ...al fin, el mar 2005    5.0                5.30
4    37 og et halvt 2005    5.6                5.30

But what I like most about it (and a similar technique of using subset()) is the use of extra named arguments that get evaluated in context of the data, without having to use the somewhat verbose syntax of a new closure and a data.frame() internal call.  So for the simpler case of by()-style / GROUP BY-style aggregation, instead of the usual

> ddply(d, .(year), function(x) data.frame(mean_rating = mean(x$year)))
  year mean_rating
1 2000        2000
2 2005        2005

I'd like to use the syntax

> ddply(d, .(year), newdf, mean_rating = mean(year))

... I wrote that newdf() myself to make the above work, like so:

newdf = function(.data, ...) { 
  e = eval(substitute(list(...)), .data, parent.frame())
  data.frame(e)
}

... But, I suspect such a function might already exist, and in any case I'm new to R meta-ish programming and wrote that just by hacking up the transform() source.

Does anyone whether I'm re-inventing the wheel?

Thanks, Brendan

--
Brendan O'Connor - http://anyall.org

parts:
You could do

> ddply(d, .(year), numcolwise (mean))
year rating

or

> ddply(d, .(year), colwise (mean, "rating"))
year rating

Hm. the use of key1=val, key2=val arguments is a lot like list() and
data.frame(); the only other similar functions i can think of are
transform() and maybe subset().

I guess if you're using it on its own, it's a lot like transform()
except it makes a brand new dataframe of any size (presumably
collapsed) instead of adding columns to the preexisting one.

How about "reframe()". (its input could be a list() or environment,
so that's not a perfect name, but usually it'll be a data frame and
it's slightly cute besides :) )

other ideas i had were:
* collapse() describes how i imagine i'd always use it, but it could
potentially expand as well.
* dfeval()
* make.data.frame()
* newframe()

By the way, here's another fun thing you can do with it:
simultaneously construct quantiles on multiple different variables
with named prefixes. i'm not sure why this works but i like it:

> ddply(head(movies,10000), .(year), reframe, r=as.list(quantile(rating)), v=as.list(quantile(votes)))
year r.0. r.25. r.50. r.75. r.100. v.0. v.25. v.50. v.75. v.100.

110 2003 1.7 5.3 6.4 7.4 9.7 5 10 27.0 138.50 31525
111 2004 1.0 5.5 6.7 7.7 9.9 5 11 24.5 131.50 22975
112 2005 1.9 5.2 6.7 8.2 9.6 5 11 19.0 67.00 4560
